title: Embedding-Based Rankings of Educational Resources based on Learning Outcome Alignment: Benchmarking, Expert Validation, and Learner Performance
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to help educators identify or generate educational resources that are well aligned with intended learning outcomes while still supporting personalization and inclusiveness. The authors argue that although large language models can generate learning materials, checking whether those materials actually cover the intended outcomes is still labor-intensive and difficult to scale. To address this, they investigate whether embedding-based similarity rankings can serve as a cost-effective automated way to evaluate alignment between resources and learning outcomes, and whether such rankings are meaningful for actual learner performance.

The paper studies a framework that benchmarks several text-embedding models on a dataset of educational resources collected from YouTube across 53 topics in domains such as machine learning, Python programming, time management, first aid, and mental health. Domain experts labeled resources as accepted or rejected based on constructive alignment with intended learning outcomes. The authors compared embedding models by ranking resources according to cosine similarity and evaluating whether accepted resources were ranked above rejected ones. The best-performing model, Voyage, achieved 79% accuracy on existing resources. The same model was then applied to 264 LLM-generated resources created by six LLMs for 22 topics in Python programming and machine learning, targeting two use cases: brevity and accessibility for learners with cognitive impairments. Expert consensus validation showed 83% ranking accuracy on these generated resources.

The learner-facing part of the study involved 360 adult participants recruited online through Prolific, all without prior programming or IT experience. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups, each receiving a first-, second-, or third-ranked generated resource for one of 12 selected topics. They studied the resource for ten minutes and then completed an expert-designed multiple-choice assessment. The study was conducted in an online setting, and educators were involved both as expert labelers and as designers of intended learning outcomes and assessments.

The main conclusion is that embedding-based ranking can effectively support scalable evaluation of educational content alignment and may help teachers personalize resources while preserving learning-outcome coverage. Voyage-based rankings outperformed the YouTube baseline and other tested embedding models, matched expert judgments on generated materials, and predicted better learner performance: students using top-ranked resources scored significantly higher than those using third-ranked resources. The authors conclude that embedding-based alignment scoring is a promising bridge between AI-generated personalization and measurable learning outcomes, while noting that current evidence is still limited by topic scope, short exposure, and narrow outcome measures.

identified_tools.name: Voyage
identified_tools.description: A text-embedding model family used to represent educational resources as vectors and rank them by semantic alignment with intended learning outcomes.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarked Voyage/voyage-large-2-instruct against other embedding models to rank existing YouTube resources and then used the best-performing Voyage model to score and rank LLM-generated educational resources for brevity and cognitive-accessibility use cases.

findings.finding_summary: Among the embedding models benchmarked on 53 topics, Voyage/voyage-large-2-instruct achieved the highest average ranking accuracy at 0.79 ± 0.14, outperforming the YouTube baseline (0.59 ± 0.18). A Friedman test across 8 models plus baseline showed overall differences, χ2(8) = 142.65, p < .001, Kendall’s W = .34; Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons found Voyage significantly outperformed every other model except Gemini, where the difference was not statistically significant.
findings.measure: Ranking accuracy for accepted-vs-rejected educational resource pairs across 53 topics

findings.finding_summary: Voyage/voyage-large-2-instruct also produced the best top-of-list retrieval performance, with Precision@3 = 0.68 ± 0.25 and Precision@5 = 0.61 ± 0.25. These values exceeded all other tested models and the YouTube baseline (Precision@3 = 0.55 ± 0.31; Precision@5 = 0.51 ± 0.26).
findings.measure: Precision@3 and Precision@5 for top-ranked educational resources

findings.finding_summary: When applied to 264 LLM-generated resources across Python Programming and Machine Learning, the optimal Voyage-based ranking achieved an average ranking accuracy of 0.83 against expert consensus labels. Reported subgroup accuracies were 0.85 for brevity/Python Programming, 0.80 for brevity/Machine Learning, 0.80 for cognitive impairment/Python Programming, and 0.83 for cognitive impairment/Machine Learning.
findings.measure: Ranking accuracy of generated resources versus expert acceptance/rejection judgments

findings.finding_summary: In a three-group learner experiment, resources ranked by Voyage were associated with significantly different learner performance outcomes, χ2(2, N = 360) = 15.39, p < .001. Learners using the top-ranked resource (n = 120, mean rank = 203.0) scored significantly higher than those using the third-ranked resource (n = 120, mean rank = 158.0), while Group 1 vs. Group 2 and Group 2 vs. Group 3 were not significant after Bonferroni correction (both p = .049; α = .017).
findings.measure: Multiple-choice assessment scores after 10-minute study of ranked generated resources

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model product used to generate educational resources.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-3.5 were used to generate brief and cognitive-accessibility-oriented educational resources for Python Programming and Machine Learning topics.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-family models were among the six LLMs used to generate educational resources, but the paper reports only pooled acceptance/ranking results across all generating LLMs rather than per-model outcomes. The authors state that all LLMs produced both accepted and rejected resources, indicating variable content quality that required verification via the Voyage-based ranking system.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's Gemini family of models, used here both as a text-embedding model for ranking and as a generative LLM for creating educational resources.
identified_tools.use_case: Gemini was benchmarked as an embedding model for ranking educational resources by learning-outcome alignment, and Gemini 1.5 Flash, 1.5 Pro, and 2 Flash were also used to generate educational materials for personalization and inclusiveness use cases.

findings.finding_summary: As an embedding model, Google/gemini-1.0 achieved an average ranking accuracy of 0.75 ± 0.15 across 53 topics. In post-hoc comparisons, Voyage was favored over Gemini, but the difference was not statistically significant.
findings.measure: Ranking accuracy for accepted-vs-rejected educational resource pairs across 53 topics

findings.finding_summary: Gemini-family generative models were included among the six LLMs used to generate resources, but no per-model generation performance was reported. The paper states that all LLMs produced both accepted and rejected resources, so Gemini's generative output quality cannot be isolated beyond this pooled mixed result.

quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes a substantial empirical benchmark and an experimental learner study with random assignment across three groups (N=360), but it is not a full RCT of a single educational intervention with comprehensive causal reporting, and several results are operational benchmarking metrics rather than standardized learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows statistically significant positive effects on learner performance for top-ranked versus third-ranked resources and strong operational gains in ranking accuracy, but standardized effect sizes for learning outcomes are not reported, making educational impact magnitude unclear.
